The Great Cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) is a large, piscivorous waterbird with a Holarctic distribution, and its life-history traits reflect a slow-paced, K-selected strategy characteristic of many long-lived seabirds. Newly hatched chicks emerge from eggs incubated at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal optimum that balances embryonic development rate with the energetic constraints of the incubating adult; the incubation period itself lasts approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days]. The neonatal mass at hatching is a modest 48.5 grams [Wwb = 48.5 grams], a value consistent with the semi-altricial developmental mode of Phalacrocoracidae, though this initial weight belies the rapid growth trajectory that follows once parental provisioning commences. Field studies have documented that this species often produces a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each clutch typically containing 4 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch typically containing 4 eggs], a maximum reproductive output that is modest compared to many smaller waterbirds but is linked to the intensive biparental care required to raise cormorant chicks to independence. The relatively slow reproductive rate is a direct consequence of the high energetic demands of foraging in temperate and boreal waters.

Under the body temperature typical of active, feeding cormorants, which is measured at approximately 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], the species reaches several critical developmental milestones that define its life-cycle schedule. Fledging, the point at which young birds achieve sufficient flight-feather development for sustained aerial locomotion, occurs at 41 days after hatching [tx = 41 days after hatching], a relatively swift transition given the bird's large body size when compared to other members of the Suliformes at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. Following this, the onset of sexual maturity, or the capacity to produce functional gametes, is attained at 123 days after hatching [tp = 123 days after hatching], though this physiological readiness does not immediately translate into breeding activity, as young adults often require additional time to acquire territory and foraging proficiency at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. The period between fledging and puberty represents a critical window of somatic growth and behavioral refinement, during which mortality rates are typically highest for juvenile cormorants navigating unfamiliar coastal and inland waterways. These timing values, derived from observations reported in DawsWhit1999, provide a robust framework for understanding the species' phenology across its wide latitudinal range.

The overall pace of the great cormorant's life cycle is further underscored by its substantial lifespan, with the maximum documented longevity for wild individuals under an active metabolic body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C] reaching up to approximately 27.2 years [am = approximately 27.2 years]. This impressive duration positions Phalacrocorax carbo among the longer-lived members of the Pelecaniformes, a trait correlated with its relatively low annual reproductive investment and high adult survival rates. The extended lifespan allows for multiple breeding attempts across a lifetime, offsetting the constraints imposed by the single, four-egg clutch produced annually. Long-term field studies of color-banded birds have confirmed that individuals may remain reproductively active well into their second decade, though senescence in foraging efficiency becomes apparent in the oldest age classes. This life-history strategy, combining delayed maturity with high adult survival, is a classic adaptation to environments where food availability for chicks is unpredictable, favoring iteroparity over a single, high-risk reproductive bout.

The age at which great cormorants initiate their first breeding attempt reflects a further delay beyond the attainment of puberty, a common pattern in long-lived colonial waterbirds. The first successful brood typically occurs at 1460 days after hatching [tR = 1460 days after hatching], meaning that individuals are approximately four years old before they contribute to the next generation at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. When examined under the thermal regime of active metabolism at 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], this deferred reproduction is consistent with the hypothesis that young birds require several seasons to acquire the necessary foraging skills, secure a high-quality nesting site within a colony, and form stable pair bonds. Competition for optimal breeding ledges in dense colonies is intense, and younger birds, often relegated to suboptimal peripheral locations, experience lower fledging success, further reinforcing the selective advantage of waiting. This extended pre-breeding period, spanning over three years, represents a significant investment in somatic maintenance and learning before any reproductive payoff is realized, a hallmark of the species' conservative life-history strategy.

In terms of ultimate body size, adult great cormorants achieve a fully-grown mass that reflects their piscivorous specialization and their position as apex avian predators in many freshwater and marine ecosystems. The typical asymptotic wet weight for this species is approximately 2300 grams [Wwi = approximately 2300 grams], although the AnAge database lists a slightly higher value of 3629 grams, a discrepancy that likely arises from geographic variation across the species' extensive range or differences between the larger northern subspecies and smaller southern populations. Reaching this adult mass involves a period of sustained growth throughout the juvenile and sub-adult stages, fueled by a diet consisting primarily of benthic and pelagic fish captured during extended diving bouts. The relatively low annual reproductive rate of one clutch of four eggs per year is energetically consistent with the metabolic demands of supporting such large-body offspring through a prolonged period of post-fledging dependency. This combination of a moderate adult weight, a delayed first reproduction, and a single, small clutch per year encapsulates the conservative life-history profile of a species well-adapted to the seasonal availability of its fish prey across temperate and boreal latitudes.
